texts.textentryhtml:
1950s, Robert L. Stolper, London [1]; by 1959, acquired by Jay C. Leff (1925-2000), Uniontown, PA [2]; Judith Nash, New York [3]; 1981, sold to Peter G. Wray (1934-2016), Scottsdale, AZ (no. 7080-W) [4]. Richard Manoogian, Detroit, IL [5]; November 19, 1990, Sotheby’s, New York, lot 91. 1991, US private collection; 2013, sold to the Princeton University Art Museum.

Notes:
[1] According to correspondence with Scott Leff, dated August 2, 2020, referring to Jay C. Leff’s ledger.
[2] According to the work’s inclusion in the exhibition Exotic Art from Ancient and Primitive Cultures, Carnegie Institute, Pittsburgh, 1959.
[3] According to US private collection.
[4] According to US private collection and Sotheby’s, Pre-Columbian Art (New York: Sotheby’s, 1990), lot 91.
[5] Ibid.

These sculptures represent two distinct aspects of Pawatuns, old male deities who are thought to support the world. One Pawatun resides in a conch shell. The other represents a hybrid creature combining fish fins and the hindquarters of a crocodile; a fish nibbles at the tip of this creature’s tail. Each Pawatun is embellished with brief hieroglyphic texts, including the name of the pair’s original patron: Til Man K’ihnich (Radiant Tapir ?), sovereign of the “water-scroll” kingdom, probably located in Belize. Another text tucked under the spiral of one Pawatun’s conch shell is an extremely rare artist’s signature, stating that “Red Tapir Macaw was the sculptor.” This is the earliest known sculptor’s signature—and thus the earliest known named artist—in the Americas.
